title: The Slow Work of Thin Air
paragraphs: A traveler who arrives in La Paz, Bolivia, roughly 3,600 meters above sea level, is breathing air that still holds about 21 percent oxygen; what has changed is the pressure pushing those molecules into the lungs.
Barometric pressure falls with altitude, and because the partial pressure of a gas is its fraction times the total pressure, the oxygen available to the body falls with it.
At sea level the partial pressure of oxygen in dry air is about 160 millimeters of mercury; near the summit of Mount Everest, at nearly 8,850 meters, it is roughly one third of that.
The French physiologist Paul Bert proved this in 1878 with pressure chambers, showing that the misery of altitude came from a scarcity of oxygen molecules rather than from low pressure itself.
The body cannot change the air, so it changes itself, and the adjustments it makes over hours, days, and weeks are called acclimatization.
The word is often confused with adaptation, and the difference matters.
Acclimatization is reversible and happens within one lifetime; adaptation is the work of natural selection across many generations and is written into a population's genes.
A climber from Chicago acclimatizes; a Tibetan herder is adapted.
The first response arrives within minutes.
Small clusters of cells called the carotid bodies, lodged where each common carotid artery divides in the neck, monitor the oxygen in arterial blood.
When the partial pressure of oxygen drops, they fire more rapidly along the glossopharyngeal nerve to the brainstem, which answers by driving deeper and faster breathing.
Physiologists call this the hypoxic ventilatory response; it is why a newcomer feels breathless even while sitting still.
Extra ventilation pulls more fresh air into the alveoli and raises the oxygen pressure there, a real but partial repair.
The repair has a cost.
Breathing hard blows off carbon dioxide faster than the tissues make it, and because carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid in blood, losing it leaves the blood more alkaline.
Chemoreceptors in the brainstem that respond to acidity sense this respiratory alkalosis and read it as a sign that breathing should slow.
Two signals now compete: the carotid bodies urging more breaths and the brainstem's acid sensors urging fewer.
In the first day or two the second signal acts as a brake, and ventilation rises less than the oxygen shortage alone would call for.
The kidneys release the brake, but slowly.
Over the next several days they excrete bicarbonate, the main base in blood, into the urine, pulling the pH back toward normal.
As the alkalosis fades the brainstem stops objecting and ventilation climbs further, which is why the heaviest breathing often comes several days after arrival rather than on the first night.

The drug acetazolamide exploits this chemistry: developed as a diuretic, it blocks the enzyme carbonic anhydrase in the kidney, forcing bicarbonate out in the urine and producing a mild acidosis within hours.
The drug thus imitates several days of renal work: ventilation rises sooner and oxygen levels during sleep improve.
Its side effects are mostly harmless but memorable: tingling in the fingers and toes and a flat, metallic taste in carbonated drinks.
Acclimatization matters because its absence hurts.

Acute mountain sickness, which commonly appears above about 2,500 meters in those who ascend too quickly, announces itself with a headache plus some mix of nausea, loss of appetite, fatigue, dizziness, and poor sleep.
Occasionally it progresses to fluid in the lungs or swelling of the brain, and both can kill.

The standard advice is therefore a schedule rather than a drug: above about 3,000 meters, raise the sleeping elevation by no more than 300 to 500 meters a day, rest every third or fourth day, and descend if symptoms worsen.
The schedule works because it gives the kidneys and the slower processes described below the time they need.

A second adjustment takes shape inside the red cells, where hemoglobin's grip on oxygen is tuned by 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate, or 2,3-BPG, a small molecule the cells make as a side branch of their sugar metabolism.
When 2,3-BPG binds hemoglobin it loosens the grip, so oxygen unloads more readily in the tissues; on a graph of saturation against oxygen pressure, the curve shifts right.
Red cell 2,3-BPG rises within a day or two at altitude, and textbooks long presented this as a clean benefit.
The story is less tidy than that.
The alkalosis of early acclimatization shifts the same curve left, tightening the grip, and at extreme altitude the leftward pull wins.
That may be no accident: near a Himalayan summit the harder problem is loading oxygen in the lungs, not unloading it in the tissues, and a tighter grip helps with loading.
The slowest adjustment is the growth of the red cell mass.
Specialized cells in the kidney sense low oxygen and release the hormone erythropoietin, or EPO, which tells the bone marrow to make more red cells.
EPO rises within hours of arrival and peaks within a day or two, then drifts back toward normal while the marrow keeps working; a measurable rise in circulating red cells takes weeks.
Travelers are told that their blood thickens within days, and in a sense it does, though not for the reason they imagine: plasma volume contracts early, so the same cells sit in less fluid.
The true expansion comes later and continues for months.
The oxygen-sensing switch behind EPO, a protein called hypoxia-inducible factor, earned William Kaelin, Peter Ratcliffe, and Gregg Semenza the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
It is tempting to conclude that more red cells are simply better, and I think that is mistaken.
Each added cell carries oxygen, but it also thickens the blood, and thick blood moves sluggishly through small vessels and taxes the heart.
Past some point the slower flow cancels the extra carrying capacity, and oxygen delivery stops improving.
Native highlanders of the Andes have lived above 3,500 meters for thousands of years and carry noticeably more hemoglobin than sea-level populations.

A meaningful fraction develop chronic mountain sickness, first described in Peru in the 1920s by the physician Carlos Monge, in which the red cell count climbs so high that the blood becomes a burden.
Headaches, fatigue, bluish lips, and strain on the right side of the heart follow.
By a widely used definition, a hemoglobin concentration of 21 grams per deciliter or more in a man living at altitude marks the condition; a typical sea-level value is closer to 15.
The Tibetan Plateau tells a different story at a similar height.

Tibetan highlanders above 4,000 meters tend to have hemoglobin concentrations close to sea-level values, well below those of Andeans at the same altitude, and chronic mountain sickness is comparatively rare among them.
They breathe more at rest and move more blood through their tissues, partly because they make more nitric oxide, a gas that relaxes vessel walls.

In 2010 several research groups reported that a variant of the gene EPAS1, which encodes one of the hypoxia-inducible factor proteins, is unusually common in Tibetans and linked to their lower hemoglobin.
Four years later a comparison of genomes showed that this stretch of DNA most likely entered the Tibetan lineage from Denisovans, an extinct group of archaic humans.
In effect, Tibetan bodies have turned down the very response that sea-level visitors turn up.
The anthropologist Cynthia Beall, whose fieldwork spans both ranges, has called the two patterns distinct solutions to the same problem, and the contrast is instructive.
Andean physiology looks like a visitor's acclimatization carried on indefinitely: more red cells, then still more.
Tibetan physiology looks like something else, a settlement reached over a long time in which the body stops fighting the thin air and lives with it.
Which is better is not a question physiology alone can answer, and I am wary of any tidy verdict that one population won.
But the contrast should make us cautious about a popular assumption: that acclimatization is a short preview of what evolution would eventually deliver.

The visitor's body does what it can in the time it has, and some of what it does, pursued long enough, becomes a disease; the system was tuned for a journey of days and weeks, not for the generations of a home.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the amount of oxygen available to the body falls at high altitude because
choices: the fraction of oxygen in the air drops as the air thins with elevation
total air pressure falls while the oxygen fraction stays the same
oxygen molecules are less able to cross into the blood in cold, dry air
low pressure acts on the body in ways unrelated to oxygen
the lungs take in less air with each breath at high elevation

proof.quote: the partial pressure of a gas is its fraction times the total pressure, the oxygen available to the body falls with it

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says the air still holds about 21 percent oxygen and that barometric pressure falls with altitude; since partial pressure is fraction times total pressure, it is the pressure, not the fraction, that drops.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 1 says the fraction stays at about 21 percent.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about cold air or the blood's ability to absorb oxygen.
This is the idea Paul Bert ruled out at the end of paragraph 1.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says breathing becomes deeper and faster, not shallower.

questions.stem: The passage credits Paul Bert with
choices: discovering that the fraction of oxygen in air is about 21 percent
measuring the barometric pressure near the summit of Mount Everest
inventing the pressure chamber as a tool for studying altitude
showing that altitude sickness stems from too few oxygen molecules
proving that low air pressure itself, not oxygen, harms the body at elevation

proof.quote: the misery of altitude came from a scarcity of oxygen molecules rather than from low pressure itself

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says Bert used pressure chambers in 1878 to show that the misery of altitude came from a scarcity of oxygen molecules, not from low pressure itself.
distractorNotes: Outside the passage: the 21 percent figure is stated as a fact, not as Bert's discovery.
Wrong detail: the Everest figure in paragraph 1 is not attributed to Bert.
Half right: Bert used pressure chambers, but the passage never says he invented them.
Reversed: this is exactly the explanation Bert's work rejected.

questions.stem: The author distinguishes acclimatization from adaptation in paragraph 2 primarily to
choices: suggest that the two words are interchangeable in everyday speech
establish a contrast that the rest of the passage will develop
argue that a climber's adjustments are more impressive than a herder's
introduce the genetic evidence that will be presented in the following paragraph
explain why natural selection works faster at high altitude than at sea level

proof.quote: The word is often confused with adaptation, and the difference matters.
acclimatization is a short preview of what evolution would eventually deliver

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says the difference matters, and the passage returns to that difference at the end, when it warns against treating acclimatization as a preview of evolution. The definition sets up the contrast the whole passage builds toward.
distractorNotes: Reversed: the author says the words are often confused, which is a reason to separate them.
Outside the passage: the author never ranks the climber's adjustments against the herder's.
Wrong paragraph: the genetic evidence does not appear until paragraph 10, and paragraph 3 is about the carotid bodies.
Outside the passage: nothing is said about the speed of natural selection.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the carotid bodies
choices: are located in the brainstem, where they regulate the depth of breathing
take several days to begin responding to a drop in oxygen pressure
release a hormone that signals the bone marrow to make more red cells
respond to a rise in the acidity of the blood by slowing the rate of breathing
sit where each common carotid artery divides and monitor arterial oxygen

proof.quote: lodged where each common carotid artery divides in the neck, monitor the oxygen in arterial blood

questions.why: Paragraph 3 places the carotid bodies where each common carotid artery divides in the neck and says they monitor the oxygen in arterial blood.
distractorNotes: Wrong location: paragraph 3 puts them in the neck and says they signal to the brainstem.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says the first response arrives within minutes.
Wrong organ: paragraph 8 says cells in the kidney release EPO.
Wrong sensor: paragraph 4 gives that job to chemoreceptors in the brainstem.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if a newcomer's kidneys could not excrete bicarbonate, the newcomer would most likely
choices: continue to have ventilation held back by the alkaline brake
experience the heaviest breathing on the first night rather than later
develop a more severe metabolic acidosis than usual
stop breathing faster altogether within the first day or two of the stay
show a larger rise in 2,3-BPG inside the red cells

proof.quote: the second signal acts as a brake
The kidneys release the brake, but slowly.
As the alkalosis fades the brainstem stops objecting and ventilation climbs further

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says the kidneys release the brake by excreting bicarbonate, and only as the alkalosis fades does ventilation climb further. Take away the bicarbonate excretion and the alkalosis, and the brake, would remain.
distractorNotes: Reversed: paragraph 5 says the heaviest breathing comes after the brake is released, not before.
Reversed: the problem in paragraph 4 is alkalosis, and keeping bicarbonate would keep the blood alkaline.
Too extreme: the carotid bodies still drive extra breathing; the brake only limits how much ventilation rises.
Unrelated: 2,3-BPG in paragraph 7 is not tied to the kidneys' handling of bicarbonate.

questions.stem: The author describes acetazolamide in paragraph 5 primarily to
choices: show how a drug can hasten a correction the kidneys make on their own
argue that drugs are a poor substitute for a careful ascent schedule
warn readers that the drug's side effects outweigh its benefits
explain why diuretics were abandoned as a treatment for acute mountain sickness
introduce the role of carbonic acid in the respiratory alkalosis

proof.quote: The drug thus imitates several days of renal work

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says the drug exploits the same chemistry and imitates several days of renal work, so it is there as an example of speeding up what the kidneys already do.
distractorNotes: Wrong paragraph and too strong: paragraph 6 prefers a schedule, but paragraph 5 presents the drug favorably.
Reversed: paragraph 5 calls the side effects mostly harmless.
Outside the passage: the drug was developed as a diuretic, and nothing says diuretics were abandoned.
Wrong paragraph: carbonic acid is explained in paragraph 4, before the drug appears.

questions.stem: All of the following are named in the passage as features of acute mountain sickness EXCEPT:
choices: headache
nausea
loss of appetite
dizziness
tingling

proof.quote: a headache
loss of appetite
dizziness
nausea
tingling in the fingers and toes

questions.why: Paragraph 6 lists headache, nausea, loss of appetite, fatigue, dizziness, and poor sleep. Tingling belongs to paragraph 5, where it is a side effect of acetazolamide.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 6 as the symptom that announces the illness.
Stated in paragraph 6 in the list of accompanying symptoms.
Stated in paragraph 6 in the list of accompanying symptoms.
Stated in paragraph 6 in the list of accompanying symptoms.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the standard advice for climbers above about 3,000 meters includes
choices: taking acetazolamide at the first sign that symptoms are worsening
descending by at least 500 meters after every third or fourth day
raising the sleeping elevation by no more than 300 to 500 meters a day
remaining at 2,500 meters until the heaviest breathing has passed
raising the sleeping elevation by about 300 meters every third or fourth day

proof.quote: raise the sleeping elevation by no more than 300 to 500 meters a day

questions.why: Paragraph 6 spells out the schedule: no more than 300 to 500 meters of sleeping elevation a day, a rest every third or fourth day, and descent if symptoms worsen.
distractorNotes: Mash-up: the advice is a schedule rather than a drug, and the response to worsening symptoms is descent.
Mash-up: the rest day comes every third or fourth day; no descent distance is given.
Outside the passage: 2,500 meters is where mountain sickness commonly appears, not a holding point.
Mash-up: the limit is per day, and the third or fourth day is a rest day.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when 2,3-BPG binds to hemoglobin, it
choices: tightens hemoglobin's grip on oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve to the left
speeds the kidneys' excretion of bicarbonate into the urine
helps the lungs load oxygen more effectively near a Himalayan summit
loosens hemoglobin's grip so oxygen unloads more readily in the tissues
raises the partial pressure of oxygen inside the alveoli

proof.quote: it loosens the grip, so oxygen unloads more readily in the tissues

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says that when 2,3-BPG binds hemoglobin it loosens the grip, so oxygen unloads more readily in the tissues, and the curve shifts right.
distractorNotes: Reversed: that is what the alkalosis does, not 2,3-BPG.
Wrong paragraph: bicarbonate excretion belongs to the kidneys in paragraph 5.
Reversed: paragraph 7 says a tighter grip helps with loading, and 2,3-BPG loosens it.
Wrong paragraph: raising alveolar oxygen is the job of extra ventilation in paragraph 3.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that, near a Himalayan summit, a drug that shifted the oxygen curve further to the right would most likely
choices: reverse the alkalosis that develops early in acclimatization
make it harder for the blood to pick up oxygen in the lungs
improve oxygen delivery by helping the tissues unload oxygen more readily
raise 2,3-BPG levels inside the red cells within a day or two
have no effect, because 2,3-BPG already dominates at extreme altitude

proof.quote: the harder problem is loading oxygen in the lungs, not unloading it in the tissues, and a tighter grip helps with loading
it loosens the grip

questions.why: Paragraph 7 says a rightward shift means a looser grip, and that near a summit the harder problem is loading oxygen in the lungs, which a tighter grip helps. A further right shift would loosen the grip and work against loading.
distractorNotes: Unrelated: the curve's position does not change blood pH; the passage runs the cause the other way.
Half right: unloading would be easier, but paragraph 7 says unloading is not the harder problem at extreme altitude.
Reversed cause and effect: 2,3-BPG shifts the curve; the curve does not raise 2,3-BPG.
Contradicted: paragraph 7 says the leftward pull wins at extreme altitude.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the early thickening of a traveler's blood at altitude is mainly due to
choices: a drop in plasma volume that packs the same cells into less fluid
the peak in erythropoietin, which arrives within a day or two of reaching altitude
a slowing of blood flow through the small vessels
a surge of new red cells released by the bone marrow
the rise in 2,3-BPG inside the circulating red cells

proof.quote: plasma volume contracts early, so the same cells sit in less fluid

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says the blood thickens within days, but not for the reason travelers imagine: plasma volume contracts early, so the same cells sit in less fluid.
distractorNotes: Wrong cause: EPO does peak early, but paragraph 8 attributes the thickening to plasma volume.
Reversed: in paragraph 9, slower flow is a result of thick blood, not its cause.
Reversed: paragraph 8 says a measurable rise in circulating red cells takes weeks.
Wrong paragraph: 2,3-BPG in paragraph 7 changes hemoglobin's grip, not the blood's thickness.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a blood sample drawn three weeks after a traveler arrives at altitude would most likely show
choices: a red cell count that has returned to its sea-level value
a red cell count that has reached its final size, since EPO has stopped
an EPO level below its early peak and a red cell count that has risen
an EPO level near its peak and a red cell count that has not yet changed
an EPO level higher than on the second day and about as many red cells

proof.quote: then drifts back toward normal while the marrow keeps working; a measurable rise in circulating red cells takes weeks
The true expansion comes later and continues for months.

questions.why: Paragraph 8 gives the timeline: EPO peaks within a day or two and drifts back toward normal, while a measurable rise in red cells takes weeks. At three weeks, EPO is past its peak and the count has started to climb.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: the red cell mass is growing at that point, not returning to baseline.
Too strong: paragraph 8 says the expansion continues for months.
Wrong timing: EPO is past its peak by three weeks, and the count has had weeks to rise.
Reversed: EPO peaks within a day or two and then drifts back down.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the idea that more red cells are simply better is best described as
choices: skeptical
resigned
enthusiastic
indifferent
bewildered

proof.quote: I think that is mistaken
Past some point the slower flow cancels the extra carrying capacity

questions.why: Paragraph 9 opens by calling the idea tempting and then says plainly, I think that is mistaken, before explaining why thicker blood stops helping. That is a skeptic's voice, not a believer's.
distractorNotes: Wrong register: nothing in paragraph 9 suggests reluctant acceptance.
Reversed: the author rejects the idea rather than championing it.
Too weak: the author takes a clear position and argues for it.
Wrong register: the author explains the problem confidently, not in confusion.

questions.stem: Which new situation best illustrates the principle described in paragraph 9?
choices: A farmer who plants more seeds in a field harvests more grain every year without limit
A library buys more books than its shelves can hold and stores the surplus in a basement
A runner who trains harder each week improves steadily until a sprained ankle forces a month of rest
A city adds buses to a route until the extra buses jam the streets and riders arrive later
A factory hires additional workers, and its output rises in direct proportion to the size of its staff

proof.quote: Past some point the slower flow cancels the extra carrying capacity, and oxygen delivery stops improving.
it also thickens the blood, and thick blood moves sluggishly

questions.why: Paragraph 9's principle is that each added carrier also clogs the system, so past some point the extra capacity is cancelled by slower flow. Extra buses that jam the streets and slow riders down are the same pattern.
distractorNotes: Contradicted: the principle is that benefit stops past some point, not that it grows without limit.
Wrong mechanism: the surplus is stored, not turned into a cost that cancels the benefit.
Wrong mechanism: the setback is a separate injury, not the added effort itself slowing the whole system.
Contradicted: output rising in direct proportion is exactly what paragraph 9 says does not happen.

questions.stem: According to the passage, each of the following is true of Tibetan highlanders EXCEPT:
choices: They make more nitric oxide, which relaxes vessel walls.
Part of their DNA most likely came from Denisovans.
They carry far more hemoglobin than sea-level populations.
A variant of the gene EPAS1 is unusually common among them and linked to their hemoglobin.
They breathe more at rest.

proof.quote: They breathe more at rest
they make more nitric oxide, a gas that relaxes vessel walls
is unusually common in Tibetans and linked to their lower hemoglobin
most likely entered the Tibetan lineage from Denisovans
hemoglobin concentrations close to sea-level values

questions.why: Paragraph 10 says Tibetan hemoglobin concentrations are close to sea-level values and well below those of Andeans. The other four statements all appear in paragraph 10.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 10, sentence 3 says they make more nitric oxide, a gas that relaxes vessel walls.
Paragraph 10, sentence 5 says this stretch of DNA most likely came from Denisovans.
Paragraph 10, sentence 4 reports the EPAS1 variant and links it to their lower hemoglobin.
Paragraph 10, sentence 3 says this directly: they breathe more at rest.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 11, the word "settlement" most nearly means
choices: the gradual sinking of material to the bottom of a liquid
an accommodation reached between two opposing pressures
a payment that ends a legal dispute between two parties
a final decision imposed from outside by an authority
a village founded by newcomers in a remote place

proof.quote: a settlement reached over a long time in which the body stops fighting the thin air and lives with it

questions.why: Paragraph 11 describes Tibetan physiology as a settlement in which the body stops fighting the thin air and lives with it: an accommodation between the body and its surroundings, not a place or a payment.
distractorNotes: Settling of particles is a lab meaning of the word that has nothing to do with this sentence.
A legal settlement is another everyday meaning; nothing in the sentence involves a dispute between parties or money.
Nothing is imposed from outside; the body reaches the arrangement itself, over a long time.
This is the common sense of the word, and the Tibetans do live in villages, but the sentence describes a state of the body, not a place.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Producing more red blood cells is the single most important change that lets a person survive at high altitude
Chronic mountain sickness shows that people who live high in the Andes are poorly suited to their home and should move lower
Climbers should take acetazolamide before every ascent because the kidneys correct the blood's chemistry too slowly
Tibetan highlanders prove that natural selection always finds the same solution that acclimatization reaches
The body's short-term answers to thin air are real but limited, and they differ from long-term genetic adaptation

proof.quote: Acclimatization is reversible and happens within one lifetime; adaptation is the work of natural selection
that acclimatization is a short preview of what evolution would eventually deliver
the system was tuned for a journey of days and weeks, not for the generations of a home

questions.why: The passage walks through the body's responses to thin air over hours, days and weeks, warns that more red cells is not simply better, and closes by separating acclimatization from adaptation. Only the answer covers both halves.
distractorNotes: The author is openly skeptical that more red cells is simply better; that is the point of paragraph 9.
Too extreme and never said: the author refuses any tidy verdict about which population did better.
Acetazolamide is one detail in the passage, and the passage never says every climber should take it.
Reversed: paragraph 10 says Tibetans turned down the very response visitors turn up, a different solution.
